task: Write one sentence of your own using the word carouse. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know carouse should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: When exams ended, the med students caroused through the old quarter until the cafes opened for breakfast.
A toast is one raised glass and a sentence; carousing is what happens when the toasts stop being counted.
A feast is grand but still tablebound; carousing is louder and wilder than any feast, spilling past the table into song.

Party is the plain modern verb for celebrating in company — any volume, any hour, cake or karaoke. Carouse is party's rowdy, old-fashioned uncle: always loud, always in a group, traditionally with glasses raised and songs half-remembered. Every carousal is a party; most parties never get near carousing.

Roister is carouse's near-twin from the same old taverns: to celebrate noisily and swagger about while you do it. The shade of difference is the strut — roisterers show off, spoiling to be noticed, while to carouse is simply to be loud together; the singing matters more than the audience.
to go without — the empty table to carousing's full one
to droop through an evening no one would call festive

Gar aus was a shouted phrase, not a root that built other words — carouse (and its noun, a carousal) is the whole family. Even carousel, the merry-go-round, is unrelated: it comes from an Italian word for a jousting parade.
Carouse means to party, celebrate.

When the show finally closed after nine hundred performances, the cast caroused backstage till dawn — costume racks for dance partners, prop crowns on every head, the stage manager leading toasts from a ladder.
Carouse is celebration at full volume, and never alone: carousers come in groups, usually loud, usually singing, traditionally with glasses in hand.
You can celebrate quietly at your desk; you cannot quietly carouse.

The town archive keeps a folder of complaints from the winter of 1954, the year the curling club finally won the provincial cup.
The team, by every account, caroused for three nights straight.
They marched from house to house with a borrowed accordion, sang until windows rattled, and emptied the hotel bar of everything but vinegar.
'We were young and the cup was heavy,' one member recalled decades later, entirely unrepentant.
What strikes a modern reader is the tone of the complaints themselves: exasperated, but affectionate.
The constable's report recommends no charges, noting only that 'the singing was in tune by the third night.' The cup sits in the library now, dented on one side.
Nobody remembers how, and the last surviving team member only laughs when asked.
